title: Streaming + Proxy + Backpressure: field notes and microbench plan
content:
Purpose and scope:
This note documents ad-hoc experiments and a small planned microbenchmark suite focused on networking and streaming overheads for our serving runtime. The specific areas: HTTP vs gRPC streaming, chunking behavior (small vs large chunks), backpressure handling when client read rates slow, and added latency/cpu when an edge proxy (Envoy / NGINX) is in the path. Goal: produce repeatable numbers we can use to tune default chunk sizes, streaming flush intervals, and recommended proxy config for Dedicated/Private customers.

High-level summary (TL;DR):
- gRPC unary+stream performs better for many-concurrent short-chunk workloads; HTTP/1.1 chunked responses show higher p95/p99 tail under head-of-line (HOL) blocking when a proxy is present.
- Small chunking (<= 512B) increases CPU sys time and context switches; prefer 1-4KB chunks for token-by-token streaming in most cases.
- Envoy with HTTP/1.1 proxying introduces extra latency (~1.2–1.8ms median per-chunk) vs direct connection; using HTTP/2 or gRPC proxying reduces extra per-chunk overhead but increases memory for concurrent streams.
- Backpressure: our runtime's current async write path will continue to allocate outgoing buffers when socket send buffers are full; need to add explicit high-water marks and pause upstream KV cache flushes to avoid OOM under slow consumer scenarios.

What we ran (short log):
- Test harness: custom Go client (client/loadgen/streamtest) that can do: HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming, HTTP/2 server-push-ish streaming, gRPC server-stream, configurable chunk_size, inter-chunk-interval (ms), concurrent connections.
- Server build: serving-runtime branch `streaming-bench-v3` with model stub that emits token payload (json tokens) with configurable generation delay (0ms/5ms/20ms) to simulate model compute. Batching disabled for these tests.
- Proxy: tested direct (no proxy), Envoy (v1.30) configured as HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 pass-through, and NGINX (1.24) as chunked reverse proxy.
- Load client: 100–2000 concurrent connections, token sizes 128B, 512B, 2048B, per-token send intervals 0ms (as fast as server), 10ms, and 50ms.
- Metrics collected: client-side per-chunk latency histogram (p50/p95/p99), end-to-end response time, server CPU% and syscalls/sec, bytes_sent/sec, socket send buffer full events (from netstat/ss), and Go runtime GC pause times.

Representative results (abridged):
- 512B chunks, 1000 conns, model delay 5ms:
  - Direct HTTP/1.1 chunked: p50 6.2ms, p95 32.1ms, p99 120.4ms.
  - Envoy (HTTP/1.1): p50 7.4ms, p95 54.9ms, p99 250ms (noticeable tail growth).
  - Envoy (HTTP/2): p50 6.8ms, p95 36.6ms, p99 140ms.
  - gRPC server-stream (direct): p50 5.8ms, p95 29.0ms, p99 95.7ms.

- Small-chunk worst-case (128B), 2000 conns, model delay 0ms (network/IO bound):
  - CPU in server: +30% user/sys vs 1KB chunks; context switches x2.
  - TCP retransmits increased on low-bandwidth link emulation; p99 blew out (500ms+).

- Backpressure test (artificially slow client reading):
  - When client read window set to 1KB/s, server memory grew over 5 minutes because outgoing write path queued chunks into a per-request buffer.
  - With high-water mark implemented in experiment branch (write path returns backpressure signal upstream), memory stabilized.
  - Envoy in front masks TCP-level backpressure by buffering, so server saw fewer send-blocks but proxy used lots of memory.

Observations and explanation:
- Proxy buffering changes where memory/backpressure happens. Direct connections push back to server (good: server can slow generation). Proxies that buffer (Envoy configured with default http1 connection buffering) absorb the slow consumer and cause server to keep writing, increasing server memory pressure. For Dedicated customers we should document and optionally detect this pattern.
- HTTP/1.1 chunked has more CPU per-chunk during header/flush handling relative to gRPC streaming which uses a more compact framing. For large # of small chunks gRPC framing wins.
- Default chunk flush interval matters: very small immediate flushes (token-by-token) are fine for <1k concurrency but will crush CPU and scheduling at >2k connections.

Actionable recommendations (short):
1) Default chunk size: set recommendation to 1–4KB token payloads for token-streaming in hosted-by-default configs. Provide a runtime flag to coalesce smaller tokens for network flush efficiency.
2) Proxy guidance: for customers using Envoy/NGINX put them in HTTP/2 mode or gRPC proxy pass-through if using server-streams; add docs with config snippets to disable large internal buffers (Envoy: buffer limits, max_request_bytes) for streaming endpoints.
3) Backpressure primitives: implement per-request send buffer HWM and explicit backpressure callbacks into generation loop; for immediate safety set default HWM to 64KB.
4) Monitoring: emit metric send_buffer_bytes, blocked_write_count, and proxy_detected_buffering boolean (heuristic: consecutive writes succeed locally but remote socket shows high buffer).

Planned microbenchmark matrix (to implement as harness):
- Factors:
  - Protocol: HTTP/1.1 chunked, HTTP/2, gRPC server-stream
  - Proxy: none, Envoy-http1-proxy, Envoy-http2-proxy, NGINX
  - Chunk size: 128B, 512B, 1KB, 4KB
  - Clients: 100/500/1000/2000 conns
  - Model synth delay: 0ms, 5ms, 20ms
  - Slow consumer patterns: normal, read-sleep(50ms) per chunk, artificial 1KB/s limiter

- Metrics to output per run: p50/p95/p99 per-chunk latency, end-to-end response time, server mem RSS, server goroutines, GC pause total, send_buffer_bytes p95, proxy buffer RSS. Save json outputs per run for analysis.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How much of the p99 tail is kernel scheduling vs our Go runtime? Need to run an experiment pinned to linux perf and with GOMAXPROCS varied.
- Validate with real model (MPT-7B and Llama-2-13B) under our optimized kernel code path; model stubs may hide batching/kv-cache interactions.
- Build detection heuristics for "proxy buffering" to surface in the console (if proxy detected, recommend switching to gRPC).

Notes to self / quick commands used: (will convert into harness tasks)
- client: go run ./client/cmd/streamtest -proto http1 -addr http://host:8080/stream -conns 1000 -chunk-size 512 -inter-chunk-ms 5
- envoy: docker run -v $(pwd)/envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml envoyproxy/envoy:v1.30.0
- collect stats: ps -o pid,rss,vsz -p $PID; ss -t -o state established '( sport = :8080 )'

Attachments / references:
- links above (PR + Jira). Also see internal perf note: /confluence/perf/streaming-overview (still rough).

Conclusion (current):
We have enough signal to change our default recommendations and to add safety knobs for backpressure. Next step: implement the HWM/backpressure API + coalescing of small tokens, run full microbenchmark matrix, and create a short customer-facing "Streaming best practices" doc for Console.
